title: Scaling limits: tree diameter ~ height^(3/2); gravity caps terrestrial size
look_for_in_this_kingdom: sauropod, proboscidean and other fossil limb dimensions with mass estimates, Carboniferous giant arthropods and trees, maximum body size through time
variables_needed: tree height and trunk diameter per tree
limb-bone circumference or cross-section against body mass
maximum body mass of land animals

claims.label: Tree trunk diameter must grow as the 3/2 power of height
claims.statement: For a tree to stand without buckling under its own weight, its diameter must increase as the 3/2 power of its height, which explains why young trees are slender and old large ones stunted, and sets a theoretical maximum tree height (about 300 ft for a Kew-flagstaff pine).
claims.quote: In general, as Greenhill shews, the diameter of a homogeneous body must increase as the power 3/2 of the height, which accounts for the slender proportions of young trees, compared with the stunted appearance of old and large ones.

Global Wood Density Database (Zanne et al. 2009, 'Towards a worldwide wood economics spectrum')
Data from: Biophysical dependences among functional wood traits (Dryad, 2019)

claims.label: Gravity sets an upper limit on the size of terrestrial animals
claims.statement: Because the strength of muscles and the crushing resistance of bones vary as their cross-section (the square of linear size) while body weight varies as the cube, there is a definite upper limit to the size of an animal living under gravity; the elephant, with disproportionately thick limb bones and reduced agility, is already near it.
claims.quote: But in a terrestrial animal the weight which tends to crush its limbs or which its muscles have to move, varies as the cube of its linear dimensions; and so, to the possible magnitude of an animal, living under the direct action of gravity, there is a definite limit set.
